meta.title: Same toy, an engineer's eye
meta.desc: A Technic-compatible Trophy truck designed the way a vehicle engineer would: 592 parts, all-wheel drive, a 3+N sequential gearbox and a piston V8 – designed with AI, modelled in Python, verified in SolidWorks.

hero.title:
Same toy,
an engineer's eye.
hero.sub: A Technic-compatible Trophy truck from 592 parts – with all-wheel drive, a sequential gearbox and a piston V8. Designed with artificial intelligence, modelled and verified one subassembly at a time.
story.title: A toy truck, with a real engineering process.
story.p1: As a kid I built suspensions and gearboxes from Technic parts. Today I'm a vehicle engineer, and my son loves LEGO too.
story.p2: The question: what happens if a toy truck is designed like a real one? The answer became a Baja-style Trophy truck: long travel, high ground clearance, all-wheel drive – from real, stock Technic parts only, and digital only.
story.p3: There is no motor. You push it, and the wheels drive the V8: through three differentials and a custom 3+N sequential gearbox, with the pistons pumping. There is no steering wheel in the cab either – it sits on the roof and drives a complete steering system.
story.s1d: independent front, 4-link rear solid axle, two shocks per wheel
story.s2d: front, centre and rear differentials, drive shafts, half-shafts
story.s3d: stepped by a roof knob: 1 → 2 → 3 → N
story.s4d: driven by the wheels, speed changing with the gear
story.s5d: from the roof, through U-joints, down to the rack
ai.title: Small steps. Every step verified.
ai.intro: A “conductor” chat plans and directs, with agents working in parallel. We went one subassembly at a time: nothing went into CAD until it worked flawlessly in the model.
ai.p1d: real parts, part numbers, dimensions from the LDraw geometry
ai.p2d: kinematics, ratios, clashes in every position, grid alignment
ai.p3d: the AI drives SolidWorks: moving mates, motion studies
ai.p4d: check tables, GO / NO-GO, human review from the STEP
ai.p5d: moving 3D on the web, video shots, finite elements
ai.c1t: Find the bug where it's cheap
ai.c1: The first, overnight CAD assembly had 223 components, but nothing moved. Since then every subassembly works in Python first – clash-free over the full suspension and steering range – and only then goes into CAD.
ai.c2: The AI can't see the screen, so it measures: the first beam's expected volume was 1300.4 mm³, SolidWorks gave 1300.6 mm³. In the final STEP, 10 random parts deviate from the model by at most 0.00002 mm.
ai.c3: Goals, decisions and the brakes. For example: stock parts only, make it a Trophy truck, and talk it through before any long process starts.
subs.title: Eight subsystems, each backed by numbers.
subs.intro: Every subsystem got its own Python model with a check table. The numbers here come from those reports. Click a figure to enlarge it.
cad.title: SolidWorks, the way the AI drives it.
cad.intro: The AI controls SolidWorks through an MCP server: it models parts, builds assemblies, adds mates, tests motion and saves images. Four subassemblies were finished with moving mates; the full truck was written to STEP from the Python model.
film.title: In motion.
film.intro: The film: 1:52, final render with narration. Next to it, the work-in-progress versions: the early animatic and two engineering shots.
film.d1: The full arc as a test render (75 s, 640×360, no sound): assembly in the virtual design space, turntable, terrain, slow motion, exploding on the move, X-ray. Made to check timing and camera work.
film.d2: The rear 12L half-shaft twisting when the wheel gets stuck (45 N·mm). FEM result: 21.6 MPa and 15.1° of twist at the wheel end. 12 s, 1080p.
film.d3: The reversed driveline turning: wheels → diffs → drive shafts → gearbox → V8. A 1 → 2 shift at 4.2 s, the roof knob turns 90°. 9 s, 720p.
film.d4: Design space, turntable, terrain, exploded view on the move, X-ray, highly serious manoeuvres, a jump, sunset. 1:52, 1080p, Hungarian narration. Rendered in Blender, motion from the Python kinematics.
film.soon: The final film is in the works – coming soon.

end.title:
Toy-sized,
with a real truck's logic.
end.text: Requirements, kinematics, gear ratios, clash checks, finite elements, CAD, moving 3D and film – one engineering process, orchestrated with AI and steered by human decisions.

next.title:
The next car
is yours.
next.intro: The same process that produced this trophy truck – idea, research, model, verification, order list, building instructions – is open to anyone. No CAD expertise or engineering background required: a good idea and a few days of persistence will do. The AI guides you through every step and hands back a result you can check at each one.
next.flow: Idea → research → 3D model → verification → order list → instructions
next.conceptsD: Three quick sketches from the same parts library, built from real Technic elements – each one took a few minutes. This is where the design work would begin: sizing, clash checks, gear ratios.

next.orderD: From the bill of materials the AI builds a BrickLink wanted list you can upload directly: part number, colour and quantity, line by line. Here is the trophy truck's list – try it.
next.how3: Choose the XML file or paste its contents, then Verify Items → Add to Wanted List.
next.how4: From the wanted list, “Buy All” finds the sellers.
next.honest: To be honest: the colours are those of the digital model, not of a retail set; real availability and prices vary. LDraw and BrickLink part numbers sometimes differ – we remapped them where we could; doubtful lines are flagged in the remarks (“CHECK ID”):
next.guideD: The 3D model is turned into step-by-step building instructions in the familiar style: the step's parts in the callout with quantities, new parts highlighted. Here are the first four steps of the front-left suspension corner.
